title: Genetic Drift
objectives: Explain random sampling of alleles.
Distinguish founder and bottleneck effects.
Compare drift with natural selection.

glossary.definition: Unpredictable change in allele frequency caused by chance sampling between generations.
A new population begins with a non-representative sample of a source gene pool.
A sharp reduction in population size that can remove genetic variants by chance.

slides.title: Inheritance involves sampling
slides.html: A generation does not transmit every allele copy equally. Chance affects which gametes form successful offspring and which individuals leave descendants. These sampling effects can change allele frequencies even when genotypes have equal expected reproductive success. Genetic drift refers to this random component of population change, rather than an individual’s deliberate response.

slides.title: Small populations fluctuate more
slides.html: If only a few allele copies form the next generation, one extra transmitted copy makes a large proportional difference. In a much larger pool, the same numerical difference changes the frequency less. Drift occurs in populations of all sizes but is generally stronger in small populations, especially when they remain small for many generations.

slides.title: A sampling model
slides.html: Imagine two founders carrying four copies at a locus. By chance, three are A, although the source pool has equal numbers of A and a. The founders begin with A frequency 0.75. No advantage for A is required: the small sample simply differs from its source.

diagram.caption: An illustrative sampling model: dots are allele copies, not people. The source is 50% A; this founder sample is 75% A.

slides.title: The founder effect
slides.html: A founder effect occurs when a few individuals establish a new breeding population with allele frequencies different from those in the source. Some rare source alleles may be absent, while others may be unusually common. Later population growth does not automatically restore the missing variants; additional mutation or gene flow would be needed.

slides.title: A bottleneck samples survivors
slides.html: A bottleneck sharply reduces an existing population. If survival is unrelated to the locus studied, the surviving gene pool may be a chance sample. A previously common allele can disappear. The term describes reduced population size and genetic consequences; not every disaster is genetically random for every trait.

diagram.caption: Hypothetical survival unrelated to the allele: A falls from 10/20 to 1/6. Real survival may also involve selection.

slides.title: Loss and fixation
slides.html: An allele is lost when its frequency reaches zero. It is fixed when its frequency reaches one, leaving no alternative allele at that locus in the population. Drift can produce either outcome without making the population better adapted. Populations experiencing different random outcomes may become genetically different from one another.

slides.title: Drift differs from selection
slides.html: Natural selection involves consistent differences in reproductive success associated with heritable traits in an environment. Drift is random with respect to the allele’s fitness effect. Both can operate together. A helpful allele can be lost by drift, particularly when it is initially rare, while a neutral allele can rise in frequency.

slides.title: Interpreting human variation
slides.html: An unusually frequent inherited condition in a small population can be consistent with founder history, drift and limited gene flow. Frequency alone does not prove the explanation or show that a community is genetically uniform. Historical records, genetic evidence and alternative explanations are needed. Broad ancestry labels cannot determine an individual’s genotype or health.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly illustrates drift?
options: A survival advantage consistently increases a heritable trait
A rare neutral allele disappears because its few carriers leave no offspring by chance
A mutation appears because organisms need it
All populations acquire the same helpful allele
feedback: Consistent trait-associated success indicates selection.
Correct: chance loss without a fitness difference is drift.
Mutation does not arise in response to need.
Drift produces unpredictable, not necessarily identical, outcomes.
questions.explanation: Correct: chance loss without a fitness difference is drift.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a founder effect?
options: A new population starts from a small sample of another population
An entire species must become extinct
Every founder has a new mutation
A large population always gains diversity
feedback: Correct: the initial sample can have unusual allele frequencies.
Extinction is not required.
Existing variants can produce a founder effect.
A small founding sample may lose diversity.
questions.explanation: Correct: the initial sample can have unusual allele frequencies.

questions.prompt: After a random bottleneck, 3 of 12 surviving allele copies are A. What is A frequency?
questions.hint: Divide A copies by all surviving copies.
questions.explanation: 3/12 = 0.25. The earlier frequency is not needed to calculate the surviving frequency.

questions.prompt: Which statement about fixation is correct?
options: It proves an allele is the most adaptive
It means a frequency of 0.50
It means one allele has frequency 1 at the locus
It creates a second allele
feedback: Drift can fix neutral or disadvantageous alleles.
At 0.50 another allele can still be equally frequent.
Correct: no alternative allele remains at that locus in that population.
Fixation removes alternative variation at the locus.
questions.explanation: Correct: no alternative allele remains at that locus in that population.

questions.prompt: Compare founder and bottleneck effects, including their shared consequence.
questions.model: A founder effect starts when a few individuals establish a new population from a source population. A bottleneck reduces the size of an existing population. Both can leave a small, non-representative sample of the original allele pool. Consequently, allele frequencies may shift and some variants may be lost by chance. Neither process necessarily increases adaptation, and later growth alone does not recreate lost alleles.
criteria: Explains loss of variation without guaranteed adaptation

questions.prompt: A beneficial allele is lost from a small population. Explain why this does not contradict natural selection.
questions.model: Natural selection describes differences in expected reproductive success, not a guarantee that every beneficial allele survives. A rare allele may be carried by very few individuals. Chance events can prevent those carriers from reproducing, eliminating the allele despite its potential advantage. Drift and selection operate together, with random sampling particularly influential in small populations. The loss therefore reflects the realised sample rather than proof that the allele lacked benefit.
criteria: Connects rarity and small samples to chance loss
Recognises selection and drift can coexist

summary: Drift changes frequencies through chance sampling.
Founders and bottlenecks can produce non-representative gene pools.
Fixation or loss does not demonstrate adaptation.
sourceNotes: Original teaching based on Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017), chapter 11 scope; source wording and questions are not reproduced.

title: Microevolution
objectives: Define evolution at population scale.
Compare mutation, selection, drift and gene flow.
Explain resistance without need-directed mutation.

glossary.definition: Change in allele frequencies within a population across generations.
An inherited characteristic shaped by selection that contributes to reproductive success in a particular environment.
An environmental influence associated with differential survival or reproduction.

slides.title: Change across generations
slides.html: Microevolution is change in allele frequencies within populations over generations. It is measured by comparing a defined locus in a defined population at different times. A person growing stronger through training is not, by that fact alone, undergoing population evolution. The relevant change concerns inherited variants and their representation in later generations.

slides.title: Mutation introduces sequence variation
slides.html: Mutation can generate new alleles through changes to DNA. A variant may affect a gene product, gene regulation or neither in a way that matters under current conditions. Mutations do not occur because an organism needs a particular solution. Only variants transmitted to descendants can contribute to the inherited gene pool over generations.

diagram.caption: Illustrative coding-strand sequences are written 5′ to 3′. One substitution introduces a sequence variant; no advantage is implied.

slides.title: Selection changes reproductive contributions
slides.html: Natural selection occurs when heritable differences lead to differences in reproductive success. An allele associated with a favourable phenotype may contribute more copies to the next generation. The advantage depends on the environment and other genes. Selection acts through individuals’ phenotypes, while the resulting evolutionary change is described at population level.

slides.title: Drift changes frequencies by chance
slides.html: Genetic drift results from random sampling of alleles in successful offspring. It does not consistently favour an environmental advantage. Its effects are especially strong when few individuals breed. A population’s allele frequencies can therefore change even if the alternatives have equal expected effects on survival and reproduction.

slides.title: Gene flow connects populations
slides.html: Gene flow transfers alleles between populations when migrants or gametes contribute to reproduction. It may introduce locally absent variants or alter their proportions. This is different from mutation, which generates sequence change. Flow can increase variation within a population while reducing differences between connected populations.

slides.title: Resistance as population change
slides.html: In a hypothetical insect population, some inherited variants confer pesticide resistance before exposure. Pesticide kills a higher proportion of susceptible insects. Resistant survivors contribute disproportionately to later generations, increasing resistance-associated alleles. The population changes; the pesticide does not instruct each susceptible insect to manufacture the useful allele.

diagram.caption: Invented allele-copy frequencies illustrate an increase under selection. These are not pesticide trial data or a prediction of a specific rate.

slides.title: Recombination is not a new allele source
slides.html: Meiosis and fertilisation combine existing alleles in new genotypes. This creates important variation among offspring but does not, by ordinary reshuffling alone, create new DNA sequence alleles or require allele frequencies to change. Distinguish a new combination of variants from a new variant itself when explaining the origin of diversity.

slides.title: Several mechanisms can act together
slides.html: A resistance allele may arise by mutation, arrive by gene flow, increase under selection and fluctuate through drift. These explanations address different steps and can all apply to one history. Frequency change alone is insufficient to identify its cause. Repeated observations, population size, movement and trait-associated reproductive success help distinguish mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Which measurement demonstrates microevolution?
options: One person gains muscle
A taught skill improves
An allele rises from 0.20 to 0.35 across generations
A chromosome is copied before mitosis
feedback: Training changes an individual phenotype, not necessarily inherited frequencies.
Learning alone does not establish allele-frequency change.
Correct: this is a population allele-frequency change.
Accurate copying need not change population frequencies.
questions.explanation: Correct: this is a population allele-frequency change.

questions.prompt: What is the ultimate source of a new DNA sequence allele?
options: Mutation
Dominance
Random mating alone
Counting a larger sample
feedback: Correct: mutation changes sequence.
Dominance describes a phenotype relationship.
Random mating reshuffles existing copies.
Sampling reveals variation rather than creating it.
questions.explanation: Correct: mutation changes sequence.

questions.prompt: Why can resistance increase after pesticide exposure?
options: All exposed insects deliberately alter DNA
Susceptible survivors must become resistant
The pesticide makes only useful mutations
Inherited resistance can increase reproductive success under exposure
feedback: Mutation is not directed by an insect’s needs.
Individuals need not change genotype for frequencies to shift.
Mutations are not restricted to useful outcomes.
Correct: differential contribution increases inherited resistance.
questions.explanation: Correct: differential contribution increases inherited resistance.

questions.prompt: Which statement about mechanisms is accurate?
options: Drift always improves adaptation
Gene flow and selection can operate in the same population
Recombination always changes allele frequencies
Selection creates the variant it needs
feedback: Drift is random with respect to fitness.
Correct: evolutionary mechanisms are not mutually exclusive.
New combinations can form without frequency change.
Mutation produces sequence variants; selection changes their contributions.
questions.explanation: Correct: evolutionary mechanisms are not mutually exclusive.

questions.prompt: Explain pesticide resistance using variation, inheritance and differential reproduction.
questions.model: A population contains heritable variation, including resistance-associated variants that may already exist before exposure. Pesticide acts as a selection pressure: susceptible insects are more likely to die before reproducing. Resistant insects therefore leave a larger share of surviving offspring, which can inherit their variants. Across generations, resistance alleles increase. This does not require individual insects to change their DNA in response to need.
criteria: States pre-existing or undirected heritable variation

questions.prompt: Explain why observing an allele-frequency change does not identify its cause.
questions.model: Mutation, migration, chance sampling and natural selection can all change allele frequencies. A rise could result from incoming carriers, random reproductive success or an advantage associated with the allele. More than one mechanism may operate simultaneously. Researchers need additional evidence, such as population size, migration patterns and consistent relationships between genotype, environment and reproductive success, before attributing the change to selection alone.

summary: Microevolution concerns inherited frequency change across generations.
Mutation, selection, drift and gene flow have distinct roles.
Resistance does not require mutation directed by need.
sourceNotes: Original teaching based on Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017), chapter 12 scope; source wording and questions are not reproduced.

title: Tay-Sachs Disease
objectives: Link HEXA variants to lysosomal dysfunction.
Apply autosomal recessive inheritance.
Explain population frequency using founder history.

glossary.definition: A gene encoding the alpha subunit needed for beta-hexosaminidase A activity.
A membrane-bound cellular compartment that breaks down particular biological materials.
An individual carrying two different variants of the same gene, one on each homologue.

slides.title: A gene-to-cell example
slides.html: Tay-Sachs disease illustrates a connection between inherited DNA variants, enzyme function and cell damage. Pathogenic variants in HEXA reduce activity of beta-hexosaminidase A. This enzyme participates in lysosomal breakdown of GM2 ganglioside, a lipid-containing molecule. Inadequate breakdown allows GM2 to accumulate, particularly affecting nerve cells.

slides.title: Lysosomal accumulation
slides.html: A lysosome normally helps recycle cellular materials through enzyme-catalysed reactions. If one required reaction is severely impaired, its substrate can accumulate even while other enzymes continue functioning. Tay-Sachs is therefore described as a lysosomal storage disorder. The location of accumulation and the cells most affected help connect molecular changes to the phenotype.

diagram.caption: A simplified mechanism: the connecting steps are explained in the accompanying text.

slides.title: Autosomal recessive inheritance
slides.html: HEXA lies on chromosome 15, an autosome. Disease generally requires pathogenic variants affecting both copies of the gene. A person carrying one pathogenic variant is usually an unaffected carrier. The two disease-associated variants need not be identical: an affected person may be homozygous for one variant or compound heterozygous for two different variants.

slides.title: A carrier cross
slides.html: In a simplified model, let A represent a functional allele and a a particular pathogenic allele. Two Aa carriers can produce AA, Aa or aa offspring. Each pregnancy has a one-quarter probability of aa, one-half Aa and one-quarter AA. These are independent probabilities, not a guarantee of one child of each type in a family of four.

diagram.caption: Schematic alleles at the HEXA locus, not whole chromosome bands. The Aa cross models one pathogenic variant; different pathogenic variants can also combine.

slides.title: Enzyme activity and severity
slides.html: The amount of residual enzyme activity helps explain the broad clinical spectrum, including infantile, juvenile and later-onset forms. Severe early disease involves progressive loss of neurological function. A disease label does not identify one identical course in every affected person. For this chapter, the important mechanism is impaired breakdown rather than memorising a fixed age of onset.

slides.title: Founder history and frequency
slides.html: If a small founding group happens to include a pathogenic allele, that allele may be more frequent in descendants than in the source population. Drift and restricted gene flow can reinforce the difference. This population-genetic explanation does not require the allele to be beneficial, and does not imply that every member of a community carries it.

slides.title: From population to individual
slides.html: Some populations have historically higher frequencies of particular HEXA variants, but ancestry cannot establish an individual’s genotype. Carrier frequency, disease incidence and allele frequency are different quantities. Under a simplified recessive equilibrium model, disease frequency is q² and carrier frequency is 2pq; these estimates require justified assumptions and do not replace individual testing.

slides.title: Testing and interpretation
slides.html: Enzyme assays and genetic testing address related but different questions: functional activity and sequence variation. Results need interpretation in clinical context. Family history may suggest inherited risk but does not by itself determine genotype. In an educational explanation, separate molecular cause, inheritance probability and population history rather than treating one as proof of the others.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best explains Tay-Sachs disease?
options: Extra haemoglobin causes muscle growth
Reduced hexosaminidase A activity impairs GM2 breakdown
HEXA variants remove every lysosome
A dominant allele prevents all DNA replication
feedback: The central mechanism involves lysosomal lipid breakdown, not haemoglobin.
Correct: impaired GM2 degradation causes lysosomal accumulation.
The lysosomes can be present but lack sufficient enzyme activity.
The inheritance and molecular target are different.
questions.explanation: Correct: impaired GM2 degradation causes lysosomal accumulation.

questions.prompt: In a simplified Aa × Aa carrier cross, what is the probability of aa in each pregnancy?
questions.hint: Use one-half a from each parent, multiplied together.
questions.explanation: Probability = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 for each pregnancy.

questions.prompt: Which statement corrects the claim that every affected person must have two identical HEXA variants?
options: Only one pathogenic copy is ever needed
Chromosome 15 is a sex chromosome
Two different pathogenic HEXA variants can occur, one on each homologue
Alleles cannot differ between homologues
feedback: Tay-Sachs is ordinarily autosomal recessive.
Chromosome 15 is an autosome.
Correct: this is compound heterozygosity.
Corresponding loci can carry different sequence variants.
questions.explanation: Correct: this is compound heterozygosity.

questions.prompt: A pathogenic allele is unusually frequent after a small founding event. What can explain this?
options: Founder sampling followed by drift
The community deliberately produced the allele
The allele must benefit every carrier
Every person in the community is affected
feedback: Correct: a non-representative founder sample can raise a variant’s frequency.
Sequence variation is not intentionally generated by a population.
High frequency does not by itself prove benefit.
Population frequency does not determine every person’s genotype.
questions.explanation: Correct: a non-representative founder sample can raise a variant’s frequency.

questions.prompt: Explain how a HEXA variant can lead to neurological damage, identifying the intermediate cellular steps.
questions.model: Pathogenic HEXA variants can reduce activity of beta-hexosaminidase A, an enzyme involved in lysosomal GM2 ganglioside breakdown. When this reaction is impaired, GM2 accumulates rather than being adequately degraded. The resulting lysosomal storage disrupts cell function, particularly in neurons, contributing to progressive neurological dysfunction. The explanation links a DNA change to altered enzyme activity and cellular accumulation before reaching the organism-level effects.
criteria: Connects cell dysfunction to neurological effects

questions.prompt: Explain why a higher population frequency of a Tay-Sachs-associated variant does not prove that it is advantageous.
questions.model: A small founding group may carry an unusually high proportion of a pathogenic variant by chance. Drift can maintain or increase that proportion, especially when gene flow is limited. These mechanisms do not depend on a survival advantage. Establishing selection would require evidence of differential reproductive success associated with the variant, rather than frequency alone. The population pattern also does not establish any particular person’s genotype.
criteria: Distinguishes frequency from evidence of advantage
Avoids inferring individual genotype from group membership

summary: HEXA variants impair lysosomal GM2 breakdown.
Autosomal recessive disease can involve identical or different pathogenic variants.
Founder history can alter frequencies without conferring an advantage.
sourceNotes: Original teaching based on Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017), chapter 13 scope; source wording and questions are not reproduced.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1218/ — gene, enzyme, inheritance and residual-activity spectrum checked; corrected the source claim that all affected people must be homozygous.

title: Sickle Cell Anaemia
objectives: Connect an HBB substitution to haemoglobin behaviour.
Distinguish sickle cell trait from HbSS disease.
Explain context-dependent heterozygote advantage.

glossary.definition: A beta-globin variant whose deoxygenated form can polymerise.
The HbAS condition, with one HbA and one HbS allele.
Higher reproductive fitness of a heterozygote than either corresponding homozygote in a particular environment.

slides.title: A sequence-to-function example
slides.html: Sickle cell anaemia provides a clear example of how a small DNA change can affect a protein and whole-organism function. An HBB variant changes a beta-globin amino acid from glutamic acid to valine. The resulting haemoglobin S differs in its behaviour from haemoglobin A, especially when oxygen availability is low.

slides.title: From DNA to amino acid
slides.html: The familiar coding-strand example changes GAG to GTG. Its RNA equivalent changes GAG to GUG, replacing a glutamic acid codon with a valine codon. This is a substitution, not a frameshift: the reading frame is retained. A single changed amino acid can alter protein interactions even though most of the sequence remains unchanged.

diagram.caption: Coding-strand triplets are shown 5′ to 3′. The corresponding mRNA triplets are GAG and GUG; this substitution changes glutamic acid to valine.

slides.title: Protein interactions affect cells
slides.html: Deoxygenated haemoglobin S can assemble into polymers that distort red blood cells. Repeated distortion damages membranes and makes cells less flexible. Reduced flexibility and interactions with blood vessels can impair blood flow. Faster destruction of red blood cells also reduces their number, contributing to anaemia and reduced oxygen delivery.

slides.title: Trait and disease are different
slides.html: HbAS describes sickle cell trait: one allele for haemoglobin A and one for S. HbSS describes sickle cell anaemia. The wider term sickle cell disease also includes some combinations of HbS with other pathogenic haemoglobin variants. Thus a simple HbA/HbS cross is useful for inheritance, but does not cover every disease genotype.

slides.title: The level of phenotype matters
slides.html: Both haemoglobin A and S can be produced in HbAS individuals, so the proteins reveal expression of both alleles. Yet HbAS is usually much less severe than HbSS. Dominance language must specify the phenotype being discussed. It is misleading to assume all heterozygous red cells are permanently sickled or that one label describes every biological level.

slides.title: Malaria changes the selective context
slides.html: In environments with substantial malaria pressure, HbAS can provide protection against severe malaria compared with HbAA. This is partial protection, not immunity, and it does not mean HbSS disease is generally advantageous. When both homozygotes have lower fitness than the heterozygote in that setting, selection can help maintain both alleles.

slides.title: A balanced polymorphism
slides.html: The sickle allele can persist even though HbSS has serious consequences because its effects depend on genotype and environment. The advantage of HbAS in a malaria setting can counter selection against HbSS. The outcome is not that every individual becomes heterozygous; reproduction continually generates different genotypes.

rows: No HbS; susceptible to severe malaria in a malaria environment
Trait; partial protection against severe malaria
Sickle cell anaemia; substantial health burden
diagram.caption: Qualitative comparison, not numerical fitness data. Actual outcomes depend on environment, care and other factors.

slides.title: Interpreting allele distributions
slides.html: Historical malaria, migration, population history and medical care can all influence observed patterns. A geographical correlation alone cannot measure each mechanism’s contribution. Modern ancestry categories are not a genetic diagnosis. When writing an evolutionary explanation, identify the allele, genotype, selective environment and reproductive consequences instead of describing a whole population as uniformly resistant.

questions.prompt: A coding DNA triplet changes from GAG to GTG. What type of mutation is this?
options: A base substitution
A whole-chromosome duplication
A one-base insertion
A frameshift caused by deletion
feedback: Correct: one base is replaced without changing sequence length.
Only a triplet substitution is shown.
No base has been added.
No deletion or reading-frame shift is shown.
questions.explanation: Correct: one base is replaced without changing sequence length.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes sickle cell trait?
options: It is always identical to HbSS disease
It is HbAS and can provide partial protection against severe malaria
It prevents every malaria infection
It means no haemoglobin A is produced
feedback: HbAS and HbSS have different haemoglobin combinations and usual severity.
Correct: trait is the heterozygous condition and protection is incomplete.
Protection against severe disease is not complete immunity.
HbAS can produce both haemoglobin A and S.
questions.explanation: Correct: trait is the heterozygous condition and protection is incomplete.

questions.prompt: How can haemoglobin S impair blood flow?
options: It removes all DNA from blood vessels
It converts red cells into neurons
Its deoxygenated polymers can reduce red-cell flexibility
It increases every cell’s oxygen supply
feedback: That is not the molecular mechanism.
The cells retain their lineage.
Correct: polymerisation and membrane damage can impede circulation.
Impaired flow can instead reduce oxygen delivery.
questions.explanation: Correct: polymerisation and membrane damage can impede circulation.

questions.prompt: For an HbAS × HbAS cross using only A and S, what is the probability of HbSS?
questions.hint: Each parent has a one-half probability of passing S.
questions.explanation: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 per pregnancy.

questions.prompt: Explain why malaria can help maintain the HbS allele despite the health burden of HbSS.
questions.model: In a malaria environment, HbAS individuals can have a survival advantage through partial protection against severe malaria. HbAA lacks this particular protection, while HbSS causes sickle cell anaemia. If HbAS has higher reproductive fitness than either homozygote in that environment, selection can maintain both alleles. The benefit depends on genotype and environment, so the explanation does not imply that HbSS is beneficial or that HbAS gives complete immunity.
criteria: Links context-dependent fitness to persistence of both alleles

questions.prompt: Trace the connection between the HBB substitution and reduced oxygen delivery.
questions.model: The HBB substitution changes a beta-globin amino acid and produces haemoglobin S. Under deoxygenated conditions, haemoglobin S can polymerise. This distorts red cells and, through repeated damage, reduces their flexibility. Blood flow can be obstructed, limiting oxygen delivery to tissues. Accelerated red-cell destruction also contributes to anaemia. The effect therefore involves changed protein interactions, changed cell properties and consequences for circulation.
criteria: Links impaired flow or haemolysis to oxygen delivery

summary: A substitution can change protein interactions without a frameshift.
HbAS trait differs from HbSS disease.
Malaria-related heterozygote advantage is conditional and incomplete.
sourceNotes: Original teaching based on Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017), chapter 14 scope; source wording and questions are not reproduced.
https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1377/ — checked HbAS advantage against malaria; source immunity wording and simplified codominance claims corrected.

title: Thalassemia
objectives: Compare alpha- and beta-globin production defects.
Explain why alpha inheritance needs four-copy accounting.
Link reduced globin synthesis to anaemia and population variation.

glossary.definition: Inherited conditions involving reduced production of alpha- or beta-globin chains.
A protein subunit of haemoglobin; adult haemoglobin A contains two alpha and two beta chains.
The number of functional gene copies contributing to a product.

slides.title: Haemoglobin needs balanced chains
slides.html: The main adult haemoglobin, haemoglobin A, contains two alpha-globin and two beta-globin chains. Each chain associates with a haem group that binds oxygen. Thalassemias reduce production of one globin type. This differs from the classic sickle variant, where a changed amino acid alters the behaviour of a produced beta-globin chain.

slides.title: Too few matching partners
slides.html: When one chain type is produced inadequately, the balance between globin partners is disturbed. Red-cell development and survival can be impaired, reducing effective haemoglobin and contributing to anaemia. Severity varies with the affected genes and residual production. It is therefore inaccurate to describe every thalassemia genotype as causing the same phenotype.

slides.title: Beta-globin inheritance
slides.html: HBB lies on chromosome 11, with one copy on each homologue in a typical diploid cell. Pathogenic variants can reduce or prevent beta-globin production. A person with one affected copy often has a trait with relatively mild effects; two disease-associated copies may cause more substantial disease. The two variants need not be identical.

slides.title: Alpha-globin has four usual copies
slides.html: Alpha-globin is encoded by HBA1 and HBA2 on each chromosome 16. A typical diploid person therefore has four alpha-globin gene copies, rather than two. Many alpha-thalassemias involve deletions or inactivation of these copies. How many functioning copies remain is important, although the specific variant and arrangement also matter.

diagram.caption: A simplified gene map: two alpha-globin loci occur on each chromosome 16 homologue, giving four copies in total. Spacing is not to scale.

slides.title: Gene dosage and severity
slides.html: Loss of one alpha-globin copy often has a smaller effect than loss of several. Loss or inactivation of three copies commonly causes HbH disease; loss of all four causes a very severe condition. These examples illustrate gene dosage, not a claim that every variant with the same copy count has an identical clinical outcome.

slides.title: Arrangement changes inheritance
slides.html: Two affected alpha-globin copies may lie together on one chromosome or one on each homologue. Both arrangements can leave two working copies in the individual, but their gametes differ. A chromosome carrying two affected loci can be passed on as a unit. Family risk therefore depends on arrangement as well as the total affected-copy count.

diagram.caption: Schematic diploid arrangements: the vertical bar separates homologues; α is a functional alpha-globin copy and − a deleted/inactivated copy.

slides.title: From red cells to phenotype
slides.html: Reduced effective haemoglobin and impaired red-cell production can produce fatigue and pallor through anaemia. More severe forms can have wider effects. Clinical management depends on the exact condition and severity, so one treatment schedule cannot describe all thalassemias. The chapter’s central principle is the connection between inherited chain production and red-cell function.

slides.title: Population history and selection
slides.html: Thalassemia-associated variants differ in frequency among populations. Migration transfers variants, and founder history or drift can change local proportions. In some malaria settings, selection has also favoured particular carrier states. These mechanisms are not interchangeable and must be supported with evidence. Ancestry alone cannot establish a person’s globin genotype or condition.

questions.prompt: What is the principal molecular distinction of thalassemia?
options: Every haemoglobin chain is replaced by DNA
Production of a globin chain type is reduced
Only red-cell shape can change
Every case deletes chromosome 11
feedback: Haemoglobin is a protein complex, not DNA.
Correct: reduced alpha- or beta-chain production is central.
Production and survival are also affected.
Variants can affect particular genes without deleting a chromosome.
questions.explanation: Correct: reduced alpha- or beta-chain production is central.

questions.prompt: A typical diploid person has HBA1 and HBA2 on each chromosome 16. How many alpha-globin gene copies is that?
questions.hint: Count two genes on each of two homologues.
questions.explanation: 2 loci × 2 homologues = 4 copies.

questions.prompt: Why can two individuals with two affected alpha-globin copies have different reproductive risks?
options: Their cells cannot undergo meiosis
All affected copies are dominant
The affected copies can be arranged in cis or trans
A gene’s chromosome never affects inheritance
feedback: Meiosis is not generally prevented by this arrangement.
Dominance does not describe the copy arrangement.
Correct: together versus separate homologues changes possible gametes.
Which copies travel together on a chromosome can matter.
questions.explanation: Correct: together versus separate homologues changes possible gametes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about population frequency is best?
options: An ancestry label proves a person has thalassemia
Migration can never move globin variants
Every high-frequency variant must be advantageous
Selection, drift and gene flow can all contribute, requiring separate evidence
feedback: Population patterns do not establish individual genotype.
Reproducing migrants can transfer these variants.
Founder effects and drift can also raise frequencies.
Correct: several mechanisms can contribute to observed patterns.
questions.explanation: Correct: several mechanisms can contribute to observed patterns.

questions.prompt: Compare alpha- and beta-thalassemia at the gene and protein-production levels.
questions.model: Both involve reduced production of a globin chain type, disturbing the balance needed for haemoglobin. Beta-thalassemia concerns HBB on chromosome 11, normally represented by two diploid copies. Alpha-thalassemia concerns HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16, normally giving four copies. Alpha disease therefore needs copy-number and arrangement accounting. Specific variants and remaining production affect severity, so neither label represents one uniform genotype or phenotype.
criteria: Identifies the affected chain in each
Correctly distinguishes two HBB from four alpha copies
Connects imbalance and residual production to severity

questions.prompt: Explain why the statement “every person with thalassemia is homozygous for one recessive allele” is inadequate.
questions.model: Thalassemia includes many different variants and more than one globin-gene system. Beta disease can involve two different pathogenic HBB variants, making a person compound heterozygous rather than homozygous. Alpha inheritance involves four usual gene copies, with different numbers and arrangements affected. Some people with a carrier or trait genotype have mild effects. Accurate description therefore requires the specific genes, variants and remaining functional copies.
criteria: Recognises multiple variants and compound heterozygosity
Distinguishes trait and more severe forms

summary: Thalassemias reduce globin-chain production.
Alpha inheritance normally involves four gene copies.
Specific variants, arrangement and population history matter.
sourceNotes: Original teaching based on Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017), chapter 15 scope; source wording and questions are not reproduced.
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1435/ — alpha-globin copy number and severe copy-loss patterns checked; corrected source blanket homozygous claim.

title: Natural Selection, Speciation and Evolution
objectives: Explain selection through inherited variation and reproduction.
Distinguish geographic from reproductive isolation.
Describe possible outcomes after separated populations reconnect.

glossary.definition: Differential reproductive success associated with heritable variation in an environment.
Evolution of independently evolving species lineages, often through reproductive isolation.
Speciation associated with geographic separation that reduces gene flow.

slides.title: Variation precedes selection
slides.html: Individuals in a population differ, and some differences are heritable. Mutation ultimately introduces sequence variants, while sexual reproduction reshuffles alleles. Environmental conditions can make some phenotypes more successful at leaving descendants. Selection does not require organisms to plan, and the environment does not produce a mutation specifically because it would be useful.

slides.title: Fitness means reproductive contribution
slides.html: In evolutionary biology, fitness concerns contribution to later generations in a particular environment. Physical strength, longevity or large body size alone does not establish high fitness. A trait that improves survival but prevents reproduction may not spread. Explanations should therefore connect the phenotype to successful reproduction, rather than stopping at the phrase survival of the fittest.

slides.title: From differences to frequency change
slides.html: If a phenotype has a heritable basis and its bearers contribute disproportionately to offspring, associated alleles can increase. The population changes over generations; an individual does not evolve a new inherited genotype by trying harder. Drift and gene flow may also change frequencies, so not every observed change is an adaptation.

diagram.caption: Hypothetical allele-copy change consistent with selection, not proof of its cause. Additional evidence is needed to distinguish selection from other mechanisms.

slides.title: Geographic separation reduces exchange
slides.html: A river, mountain barrier or separated habitat can reduce contact between breeding populations. With less gene flow, mutation, drift and different selection pressures can change their gene pools more independently. This is the setting for allopatric speciation. Separation begins the opportunity for divergence; it does not instantly create a second species.

slides.title: Reproductive isolation is the key distinction
slides.html: Under the biological species concept, reproductive isolation prevents or greatly restricts gene exchange between populations. Differences may prevent mating, fertilisation or production of viable fertile offspring. Geographic isolation describes where populations occur; reproductive isolation describes barriers to genetic exchange. The two can be related, but they are not the same condition.

slides.title: Divergence without a physical barrier
slides.html: Sympatric speciation occurs within the same geographical region. Gene exchange can decrease through ecological, behavioural or genetic differences even without a large physical barrier. This is a different spatial setting from allopatry, not a different definition of evolution. The exact mechanism must explain how reproductive connections become sufficiently restricted.

slides.title: When contact resumes
slides.html: If separated populations reconnect while still reproductively compatible, gene flow may blend their differences. If strong reproductive isolation has evolved, they may remain distinct. Intermediate outcomes include limited hybridisation. These outcomes depend on the barriers and fitness of offspring; simply removing a geographical obstacle does not tell us which result will occur.

diagram.caption: A simplified mechanism: the connecting steps are explained in the accompanying text.

slides.title: A branching history, not a ladder
slides.html: Speciation can split one ancestral lineage into descendant lineages. Neither descendant must be more advanced, and both can continue evolving. A branching tree represents relationships rather than progress towards a goal. Species boundaries may require several lines of evidence, particularly where hybridisation occurs or only fossils are available.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes evolutionary fitness?
options: Being physically strongest
Living longest regardless of offspring
Contributing inherited alleles successfully to later generations
Having the largest genome
feedback: Strength can help in some settings but is not the definition.
Longevity without reproduction does not ensure genetic contribution.
Correct: fitness concerns reproductive contribution in context.
Genome size does not define reproductive success.
questions.explanation: Correct: fitness concerns reproductive contribution in context.

questions.prompt: A river separates a population. What follows immediately?
options: Two species must exist
Gene flow may be reduced
Every allele becomes fixed
All mutations become advantageous
feedback: Speciation requires further persistent divergence and isolation.
Correct: separation can reduce reproductive contact.
Isolation does not instantly remove all variation.
Mutation effects remain context dependent.
questions.explanation: Correct: separation can reduce reproductive contact.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes sympatric from allopatric speciation?
options: Sympatric divergence occurs in the same geographical region
Sympatric speciation excludes reproductive isolation
Allopatric populations can never reconnect
Only sympatric populations undergo mutation
feedback: Correct: the terms distinguish spatial settings.
Reproductive isolation remains central.
Barriers can change and contact can resume.
Mutation can occur in either setting.
questions.explanation: Correct: the terms distinguish spatial settings.

questions.prompt: Separated populations reconnect and freely produce viable fertile offspring. What is supported?
options: Separation alone guaranteed speciation
Gene flow is impossible
Their earlier divergence must have involved no genetic change
Complete reproductive isolation has not developed
feedback: Their compatibility shows that geography alone was insufficient.
Successful reproduction permits gene flow.
They may have changed without becoming fully isolated.
Correct: freely exchanging viable fertile offspring indicates compatibility.
questions.explanation: Correct: freely exchanging viable fertile offspring indicates compatibility.

questions.prompt: Explain how geographic isolation can contribute to speciation, distinguishing the two forms of isolation.
questions.model: Geographic separation reduces opportunities for gene flow. The separated populations can then diverge through mutation, drift and selection under different conditions. Over generations, some differences may become reproductive barriers, preventing mating or production of viable fertile offspring. Geographic isolation concerns physical separation, while reproductive isolation concerns restricted genetic exchange. Speciation is possible if reproductive barriers persist, but physical separation alone does not guarantee it.

questions.prompt: Explain why “the strongest individuals survive” is an incomplete account of natural selection.
questions.model: Selection requires heritable variation and differences in reproductive success. Strength is only one possible influence and may be irrelevant or costly in some environments. Survival matters when it changes contribution to later generations, but survival without reproduction does not spread an allele. A complete account identifies the varying phenotype, its inherited basis, the environmental pressure and the resulting difference in offspring contribution across generations.
criteria: Links individual differences to population change

summary: Selection acts through heritable differences in reproductive success.
Geographic separation can permit divergence without guaranteeing speciation.
Reproductive isolation and gene flow determine outcomes after contact.
sourceNotes: Original teaching based on Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017), chapter 16 scope; source wording and questions are not reproduced.

title: Allele Frequencies and Natural Selection
objectives: Calculate frequencies from observed genotypes.
Use Hardy–Weinberg predictions appropriately.
Explain how selection can change frequencies.

glossary.definition: The proportion of individuals with a particular genotype.
The proportion of copies at a locus belonging to one allele.
A model population with no gene flow across its defined boundary.

slides.title: Count before explaining
slides.html: Frequency calculations and explanations answer different questions. Counting observed genotypes can establish allele proportions directly, without assuming equilibrium. Explaining why proportions changed requires evidence about selection, drift, mutation or gene flow. Keep these stages separate: a reliable calculation does not automatically prove the biological cause of the pattern.

slides.title: A complete worked example
slides.html: In an illustrative sample of 200 people, there are 72 AA, 96 Aa and 32 aa. AA frequency is 72/200 = 0.36 and Aa frequency is 0.48. A copies total 2 × 72 + 96 = 240. There are 400 copies at the locus, so A frequency is 0.60 and a frequency is 0.40.

diagram.caption: Invented sample used to distinguish people from allele copies. Total A = 240 among 400 copies.

slides.title: Predicting genotypes from alleles
slides.html: Under the two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model, p + q = 1 and expected genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q². If p = 0.60 and q = 0.40, the predictions are 0.36, 0.48 and 0.16. These happen to match the illustrative sample, but a numerical match alone does not prove every assumption is met.

slides.title: What random mating does
slides.html: Random union of gametes determines expected genotype proportions from the allele frequencies. It does not make dominant alleles increase automatically. Without selection, mutation, migration or appreciable drift, allele frequencies can remain stable even though individual alleles are continually recombined into different offspring. Dominance is about phenotype, not a built-in transmission advantage.

slides.title: Selection changes the contributors
slides.html: Suppose a heritable phenotype associated with A leaves more surviving offspring in a particular environment. The next breeding generation can contain a higher fraction of A copies. To attribute the change to selection, evidence should connect phenotype or genotype to differential reproduction, while considering migration and sampling effects as alternative or additional explanations.

diagram.caption: Invented copies illustrate a frequency rise from 0.40 to 0.65. Counts alone show change, not its mechanism.

slides.title: Recessive variants can remain hidden
slides.html: With complete dominance, a recessive allele in a heterozygote may not produce the recessive phenotype. Selection against that phenotype therefore acts directly on homozygotes, while carriers can transmit the allele. This helps explain why a harmful recessive variant may persist. It does not imply every recessive variant is harmful or adaptive.

slides.title: Open and closed populations
slides.html: A closed-population model excludes gene flow across its boundary. An open population permits reproductive contributions from outside. Neither term specifies population size, and closure does not guarantee equilibrium: mutation, selection or drift can still change a closed pool. State the boundary being used rather than assuming a geographical label establishes complete isolation.

slides.title: Assumptions guide interpretation
slides.html: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium assumes a very large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration and no selection at the locus. Violating one condition does not always mean drift: migration causes gene flow, and selection has its own mechanism. Non-random mating can alter genotype proportions without necessarily changing allele frequencies.

questions.prompt: Among 100 people there are 25 AA, 50 Aa and 25 aa. What is A frequency?
Under Hardy–Weinberg assumptions, a recessive aa phenotype has frequency 0.16. What is the expected carrier frequency?
questions.hint: Find q from q², then p = 1 − q and carriers = 2pq.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a closed population is accurate?
options: Its frequencies can still change through selection or drift
Its population must be very large
It contains no recessive alleles
It is necessarily at equilibrium
feedback: Correct: exclusion of gene flow does not exclude other mechanisms.
Closure describes exchange, not size.
Allele type is not determined by closure.
Other equilibrium conditions can fail.
questions.explanation: Correct: exclusion of gene flow does not exclude other mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Why can a recessive variant persist despite selection against aa?
options: Carriers cannot transmit it
It automatically becomes dominant
Aa carriers can transmit it without showing the recessive phenotype
Selection always eliminates variants in one generation
feedback: Carriers normally can pass either allele to offspring.
Dominance is not automatically changed by selection.
Correct: copies in heterozygotes can escape selection acting on aa.
Elimination is not guaranteed, especially for rare recessive variants.
questions.explanation: Correct: copies in heterozygotes can escape selection acting on aa.

questions.prompt: A frequency calculation shows A increased. Explain what additional evidence is needed to attribute this to selection.
questions.model: The calculation demonstrates a change but not its cause. Evidence for selection should show a heritable phenotype or genotype associated with greater reproductive contribution in the relevant environment. Researchers should also consider incoming migrants, mutation and random sampling, especially in a small population. Repeated observations and a consistent genotype–environment–reproduction relationship strengthen the explanation. Several mechanisms may contribute to the same frequency change.
criteria: Considers flow or drift as alternatives

questions.prompt: Explain why counting a dominant phenotype is different from counting A copies in an observed genotype sample.
questions.model: With complete dominance, both AA and Aa individuals can show the same dominant phenotype. However, each AA contributes two A copies while each Aa contributes only one. Phenotype frequency counts individuals and combines those genotypes; allele frequency counts copies with a denominator of twice the number of diploid individuals. Observed genotype counts permit direct calculation of A copies without assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.
criteria: Identifies AA and Aa phenotype overlap
Counts two versus one A copy

summary: Direct allele counting does not require equilibrium.
Hardy–Weinberg expectations are conditional predictions.
Selection must be connected to differential reproductive contributions.
sourceNotes: Original teaching based on Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017), chapter 17 scope; source wording and questions are not reproduced.

title: Activity — Model for Natural Selection
objectives: Interpret a model with explicit inheritance and selection rules.
Separate model results from evidence about real hominins.
Explain replication, controls and limitations.

glossary.definition: A simplified representation used to explain or investigate a process.
An independent repetition used to examine variation in results.
A model instruction giving different variants different survival or reproductive probabilities.

slides.title: A model represents a mechanism
slides.html: A classroom model can represent natural selection using labelled tokens, inheritance rules and different survival probabilities. It is useful because the rules can be inspected and repeated. Tokens are not organisms, however. The model demonstrates consequences of its assumptions; it does not independently establish the causes of a real evolutionary event.

slides.title: Define what a token represents
slides.html: For a simple allele-copy model, let each token represent A or a at one locus. For a phenotype model, a token instead represents a type of individual. These interpretations cannot be switched midway through a calculation. If tokens represent individuals, an explicit inheritance rule is needed before their colours can be treated as inherited alleles.

slides.title: A transparent illustrative outcome
slides.html: Consider 20 model allele copies, initially 10 A and 10 a. A prescribed selection-and-reproduction rule produces a later pool of 20 copies containing 14 A. Frequency rises from 0.50 to 0.70. These invented values illustrate the calculation only; they are neither measured classroom results nor data about human evolution.

diagram.caption: Explicitly hypothetical model: coloured dots are A copies. Frequency = coloured copies/total copies; no historical population is represented.

slides.title: Biased rules represent selection
slides.html: A rule that gives one heritable type a higher probability of leaving descendants represents differential reproductive success. Random draws can still add variation around the expected result. If every type has equal probabilities, changes can still occur through sampling, but the model would then illustrate drift rather than selection for that type.

slides.title: Keep the comparison interpretable
slides.html: Holding the model population size constant can make frequency changes easy to compare. It does not mean real populations always remain constant. If the total changes, use proportions rather than raw numbers. A type increasing from 10 to 15 tokens has not increased in frequency if the total simultaneously rises from 20 to 40.

slides.title: Replicates reveal chance variation
slides.html: Independent runs using the same rules need not give identical outcomes. Repeating the model shows how much chance affects the result and whether a general tendency is consistent. Report the range or distribution of outcomes, not only a convenient run. Larger model pools usually reduce proportional sampling fluctuations.

slides.title: A control isolates the effect
slides.html: Compare a treatment with unequal reproductive probabilities against a control with equal probabilities. Keep the inheritance rule, initial composition and population size consistent. A stronger treatment–control difference supports the role of the prescribed bias within the model. It still does not show that the same numerical probabilities applied to real organisms.

diagram.caption: A simplified mechanism: the connecting steps are explained in the accompanying text.

slides.title: Do not model a ladder of humans
slides.html: Assigning different hominin species to colours and favouring a larger brain can misleadingly imply a single breeding population or inevitable progress. Distinct species are not simply alleles at one locus, and brain size alone does not establish fitness. Use neutral A/a labels for the mechanism and separate real evolutionary claims from the teaching model.

questions.prompt: A model has 8 A tokens among 20 total tokens. What is A frequency?
questions.hint: Divide A tokens by the total, using the same token interpretation.

questions.prompt: What feature makes a model illustrate selection rather than only drift?
options: Every token has the same reproductive probability
Different heritable types have different reproductive probabilities
Only one run is performed
The tokens are very colourful
feedback: Equal success can still produce sampling changes, but no prescribed selective bias.
Correct: type-associated differential success represents selection.
The number of runs affects evaluation, not the selection mechanism.
Colour is a label unless connected to an explicit rule.
questions.explanation: Correct: type-associated differential success represents selection.

questions.prompt: Why repeat independent runs?
options: To guarantee every result is identical
To remove all chance from inheritance
To examine variability and consistency of the pattern
To turn invented tokens into fossil evidence
feedback: Random sampling can produce different outcomes.
Replication measures variation; it does not abolish it.
Correct: replication reveals chance effects around the model tendency.
Model results do not become direct historical evidence.
questions.explanation: Correct: replication reveals chance effects around the model tendency.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion exceeds what the model establishes?
options: Biased rules can change type frequencies
Changing totals requires frequency calculations
Equal-probability sampling can fluctuate
A coloured-token result proves why a particular hominin species became extinct
feedback: This is an appropriate mechanism-level conclusion.
Proportions are needed to compare changing totals.
This appropriately describes drift.
Correct: a teaching model cannot by itself prove a specific historical cause.
questions.explanation: Correct: a teaching model cannot by itself prove a specific historical cause.

questions.prompt: Explain how a control and repeated runs improve a natural-selection model.
questions.model: An equal-success control provides a baseline for changes caused by sampling alone. A treatment can then apply unequal reproductive probabilities while keeping other rules comparable. Independent repeated runs reveal variability and show whether the treatment produces a consistent tendency rather than one chance outcome. These steps improve interpretation within the model, but they do not demonstrate that its simplified probabilities describe a real population.

questions.prompt: Explain why different hominin species should not be treated simply as alleles in one freely interbreeding token population.
questions.model: Alleles are alternative sequence variants at a locus within a genetic inheritance system, whereas hominin species represent evolutionary lineages with their own histories and reproductive relationships. Treating species labels as freely mixing alleles hides those distinctions. It can also imply a ladder in which larger brains automatically win. A simple A/a model can teach frequency change, while fossil, genetic and environmental evidence is needed for specific hominin conclusions.

summary: Model rules must state what tokens and inheritance represent.
Replication and controls distinguish bias from sampling variation.
A mechanism model does not prove a particular historical event.
sourceNotes: Original teaching based on Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017), chapter 18 scope; source wording and questions are not reproduced.

title: Endonucleases
objectives: Describe which DNA bond an endonuclease breaks.
Explain sequence-specific restriction digestion.
Relate cutting patterns to fragment analysis and cloning.

glossary.definition: An enzyme that cleaves bonds within a nucleic-acid chain.
A DNA recognition sequence associated with cutting by a particular restriction enzyme.
A DNA piece generated by restriction-enzyme cleavage.

slides.title: Cutting the DNA backbone
slides.html: An endonuclease cleaves internal bonds in a nucleic-acid chain. DNA endonucleases break phosphodiester bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone. This differs from separating complementary strands by disrupting base pairing. To cut a double-stranded DNA molecule into separate pieces, cleavage must affect the backbones of both strands at appropriate positions.

slides.title: Specificity makes cutting useful
slides.html: Restriction endonucleases recognise particular DNA sequences. Many commonly used laboratory enzymes cut at defined positions at or near those sites. A DNA molecule with several sites can therefore yield several fragments after complete digestion. The pattern depends on both the molecule’s sequence and the selected enzyme, rather than on fragment purpose or usefulness.

slides.title: Recognition and cleavage are distinct
slides.html: The recognition sequence is the enzyme’s binding target; the cleavage positions specify which backbone bonds are broken. Depending on the enzyme, cuts can be directly opposite or staggered. Opposite cuts produce blunt ends, while staggered cuts can leave short single-stranded overhangs, called sticky or cohesive ends.

slides.title: Compatible sticky ends can pair
slides.html: Complementary overhangs can hydrogen-bond with one another. DNA from different sources can therefore be brought together if their ends are compatible. This pairing does not yet seal the sugar–phosphate backbones. DNA ligase is required to form the missing covalent bonds. The cutting and sealing enzymes perform different steps in assembling recombinant DNA.

diagram.caption: A simplified mechanism: the connecting steps are explained in the accompanying text.

slides.title: A bacterial defence context
slides.html: Restriction systems can help bacteria and archaea defend against foreign genetic material. In many systems, associated DNA modifications help distinguish the host’s DNA from susceptible foreign DNA. The enzyme is not deliberately choosing a useful gene: its biochemical specificity determines the target. Not every endonuclease is a sequence-specific restriction enzyme.

slides.title: Why Type II enzymes are common
slides.html: Restriction enzymes are grouped by properties including recognition, cleavage and biochemical requirements. Type II enzymes are especially useful in routine DNA manipulation because many produce predictable cuts at or near their recognition sequences. Other groups can cut farther away or respond to modified DNA. A laboratory procedure must specify the actual enzyme rather than assuming all types behave identically.

slides.title: Fragments can be compared on a gel
slides.html: After digestion, gel electrophoresis separates suitable DNA fragments mainly by size. Different restriction sites can yield different fragment patterns. A band is an observation about migrating DNA, not a direct label for a gene or phenotype. Controls and a size standard help interpretation, and similarly sized fragments may migrate together.

diagram.caption: Invented relative migration positions, not base-pair counts. Wells are at the negative/top end; DNA moves toward the positive/bottom end. Different band patterns can follow different restriction sites.

slides.title: Count sites with molecule shape
slides.html: For a simple linear DNA molecule, complete cleavage at two distinct sites yields three fragments. A circular molecule cut at two distinct sites yields two fragments. This counting assumes complete digestion and ignores fragments too small to observe. Always establish whether the starting DNA is linear or circular before inferring fragment number.

questions.prompt: Which bond does a DNA endonuclease cleave?
options: Peptide bonds joining amino acids
Hydrogen bonds only between base pairs
Phosphodiester bonds in a DNA backbone
Bonds joining all chromosomes into one molecule
feedback: Proteases act on peptide bonds; DNA has a sugar–phosphate backbone.
Strand separation alone is different from backbone cleavage.
Correct: internal backbone cleavage is the defining action.
Human chromosomes are separate molecules, not one chain joined this way.
questions.explanation: Correct: internal backbone cleavage is the defining action.

questions.prompt: What gives a restriction enzyme its characteristic cutting pattern?
options: Recognition of particular DNA sequences and cleavage positions
The researcher’s desired phenotype
The colour of the sample tube
A rule that every gene is cut once
feedback: Correct: sequence and enzyme specificity determine sites.
The enzyme does not recognise the purpose of the experiment.
Tube colour does not define the DNA target.
Genes need not each contain a site.
questions.explanation: Correct: sequence and enzyme specificity determine sites.

questions.prompt: A linear DNA molecule is completely cut at three distinct internal sites. How many fragments result?
questions.hint: For a simple linear molecule, each additional distinct cut increases the number of pieces by one.
questions.explanation: A linear molecule starts as one piece. Three cuts give 3 + 1 = 4 fragments.

questions.prompt: Compatible sticky ends have paired. What is still needed to seal their backbones?
options: Another mutation in every base
DNA ligase
Removal of all phosphates
Destruction of the complementary strand
feedback: Sequence change is not required for sealing.
Correct: ligase catalyses the missing covalent backbone bonds.
A suitable 5′ phosphate is required for standard ligation.
The paired strands provide the aligned substrate.
questions.explanation: Correct: ligase catalyses the missing covalent backbone bonds.

questions.prompt: Distinguish recognition sites, cutting positions and sticky ends.
questions.model: A recognition site is the sequence to which a restriction enzyme responds. Its cutting positions are the phosphodiester bonds it cleaves in the two backbones; these may lie at or near the recognised sequence, depending on the enzyme. Staggered cuts leave short single-stranded overhangs called sticky ends. Complementary overhangs can pair, but DNA ligase is still needed to seal the backbone covalently.
criteria: Explains overhang pairing versus covalent sealing

questions.prompt: Explain why a changed gel pattern after restriction digestion does not by itself identify a changed phenotype.
questions.model: A restriction pattern depends on recognition-site locations, fragment lengths and experimental conditions. A sequence difference may create or remove a site without affecting a gene product, while an important functional change may leave the tested sites unchanged. Bands therefore show fragment behaviour rather than directly revealing a phenotype. Appropriate controls, sequence information and functional evidence are needed to connect a pattern to a biological effect.
criteria: Connects bands to sites and fragment sizes
Explains sequence changes need not alter function

summary: Endonucleases cut internal nucleic-acid backbone bonds.
Restriction specificity allows predictable fragment production.
Compatible ends pair, while ligase performs covalent sealing.
sourceNotes: Original teaching based on Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017), chapter 19 scope; source wording and questions are not reproduced.

title: DNA Ligases
objectives: Identify the bond and end groups joined by DNA ligase.
Explain ligase action in replication and DNA assembly.
Distinguish pairing, synthesis and sealing.

glossary.definition: An enzyme that seals suitable adjacent DNA ends by forming a phosphodiester bond.
Covalent joining of suitable nucleic-acid ends.
DNA assembled from sequences that were previously separate, potentially from different sources.

slides.title: Sealing a backbone
slides.html: DNA ligase catalyses formation of a phosphodiester bond between an adjacent 3′ hydroxyl and 5′ phosphate. This joins the sugar–phosphate backbone. Ligase does not choose a gene by its biological meaning or copy a long missing sequence. It acts on suitable aligned DNA ends, with requirements that depend on the particular enzyme.

slides.title: DNA has direction
slides.html: The two strands of DNA run in opposite directions, and each strand has distinguishable 5′ and 3′ ends. Correctly oriented end groups matter chemically. When a nick interrupts one backbone in an otherwise paired molecule, ligase can seal that interruption if the required groups are present. Base pairing helps hold the ends in position.

slides.title: Why replication needs ligase
slides.html: During replication, the lagging strand is made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments. Processing removes primers and replaces them with DNA. Suitable adjacent fragments are then sealed into a continuous backbone by ligase. Polymerase extends DNA by adding nucleotides; ligase joins existing adjacent ends. Both are needed, but they perform different chemical tasks.

diagram.caption: A simplified mechanism: the connecting steps are explained in the accompanying text.

slides.title: Repair is coordinated
slides.html: DNA repair can involve cutting damaged material, filling a gap and sealing a remaining nick. Ligase performs the sealing stage, while other enzymes carry out damage recognition and DNA synthesis. It is therefore misleading to say ligase alone uses a template to replace missing bases. A complete explanation assigns each step to the appropriate activity.

slides.title: Joining previously separate fragments
slides.html: In DNA assembly, a vector and insert can be prepared with compatible ends. Complementary sticky ends can pair, aligning backbone ends for ligation. The resulting covalent molecule is recombinant DNA. Blunt-end ligation is also possible with suitable enzymes and conditions, but lacks the same overhang-directed pairing that brings sticky ends together.

slides.title: A schematic assembly
slides.html: Imagine a vector opened at one location and a separate insert prepared with compatible ends. Pairing positions the insert between the vector ends. Ligase seals the junctions; successful assembly requires appropriate bonding on both strands. The labels describe DNA regions rather than a real plasmid sequence, and the diagram does not establish whether the insert will be expressed.

diagram.caption: Schematic DNA regions: the assembled label represents covalent joining, not deletion or shortening of DNA. Compatible ends and correct end chemistry are required.

slides.title: Reaction conditions matter
slides.html: A ligation reaction needs a suitable DNA substrate, active enzyme and the required buffer components and energy source. Common T4 DNA ligase protocols use ATP; other ligases can have different requirements. Temperature affects end pairing and enzyme activity. There is no single optimal temperature that can be applied to every ligase or assembly method.

slides.title: Check the product, not just the process
slides.html: Adding ligase does not guarantee the desired construct. A vector may rejoin without the insert, or an insert may have an unintended orientation. Appropriate checks can examine junction sequences, insert size and arrangement. A correctly joined DNA molecule also does not automatically produce a functional protein; expression requires suitable regulatory and coding information.

questions.prompt: What does DNA ligase directly form?
options: A new amino acid
A phosphodiester bond between suitable DNA ends
A missing sequence by reading an RNA template
A hydrogen bond instead of a backbone bond
feedback: Ligase acts on nucleic acids, not protein translation.
Correct: this covalently seals the sugar–phosphate backbone.
Copying missing sequence is not ligase’s direct role.
Base pairing aligns ends, but ligase forms a covalent bond.
questions.explanation: Correct: this covalently seals the sugar–phosphate backbone.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is accurate during lagging-strand replication?
options: Ligase adds every nucleotide; polymerase seals nicks
Neither enzyme acts on DNA
Polymerase extends DNA; ligase seals suitable adjacent ends
Ligase removes all chromosomes
feedback: The roles are reversed.
Both act in DNA replication.
Correct: synthesis and sealing are distinct activities.
Ligase does not remove chromosomes.
questions.explanation: Correct: synthesis and sealing are distinct activities.

questions.prompt: Two sticky-ended fragments have paired but their backbones remain interrupted. Which statement is best?
options: The DNA is already covalently sealed
Ligation requires all bases to mutate
DNA polymerase is always unnecessary in repair
Base pairing has aligned them, and ligase can seal suitable ends
feedback: Pairing alone does not form the missing phosphodiester bonds.
Compatible ends can be sealed without changing their sequence.
Gap filling can require polymerase before sealing.
Correct: hydrogen-bond pairing and covalent ligation are separate steps.
questions.explanation: Correct: hydrogen-bond pairing and covalent ligation are separate steps.

questions.prompt: Why check an assembled vector after ligation?
options: Ligation can produce an unintended insert arrangement or reclosed vector
Ligase automatically proves protein function
Every vector must contain the desired insert
All ligases identify the intended gene by meaning
feedback: Correct: the physical product needs verification.
Expression and protein function need separate evidence.
Vectors can rejoin without the intended insert.
Enzyme chemistry does not recognise experimental intent.
questions.explanation: Correct: the physical product needs verification.

questions.prompt: Explain how restriction enzymes and DNA ligase can work together to assemble recombinant DNA.
questions.model: A restriction enzyme cuts DNA at defined positions associated with its recognition sequence. Cutting the vector and insert with suitable enzymes can produce compatible ends. Complementary overhangs pair and align the fragments, but the sugar–phosphate backbones remain interrupted. DNA ligase catalyses the missing phosphodiester bonds at suitable adjacent ends, producing a covalently joined molecule. The resulting construct must still be checked for the intended insert and arrangement.

questions.prompt: Explain why ligase alone cannot complete every DNA repair task.
questions.model: A damaged DNA region may first need recognition, removal and replacement. Ligase can seal a nick between suitable adjacent end groups, but it does not synthesise a long missing sequence or identify every form of damage. Polymerase and other repair proteins can be required to prepare a substrate that ligase can seal. Repair is therefore a coordinated sequence of activities, with ligation completing particular backbone junctions.
criteria: Identifies suitable adjacent ends as substrate

summary: Ligase seals suitable 3′ hydroxyl and 5′ phosphate ends.
